newsitem.title: UK: S&P AFFIRMS SEGUROS COMERCIAL AMERICA.
newsitem.headline: S&P AFFIRMS SEGUROS COMERCIAL AMERICA.

text.p: LONDON, Aug 4 - Standard & Poor's today has affirmed its triple-B' claims-paying ability rating on Mexican insurer Seguros Comercial America.

The rating reflects Seguros Comercial America's strong market position in property and casualty commercial lines and, following the Dec. 31, 1996 merger with Aseguradora Mexicana (Asemex), the company's increased profit potential over the longer term.

Asemex, which was once a government-owned insurer, operates as a division specializing in products for public sector clients. The combined company leads the Mexican market, with a share of insurance premiums exceeding 30% as of year-end 1996.
Standard & Poor's believes that Seguros Comercial America's management team has proven its ability to realize improvements in operating performance from past mergers.

Benefits from this merger include the ability to combine branch offices, expand distribution, and negotiate more favorable reinsurance programs. Seguros Comercial America's own 1996 net income was 396 million pesos (703 million pesos before prevision and catastrophe reserves), resulting in a 4.3% return on assets. As a percentage of earned premiums, net income slipped to 7.5% from 8.6% in 1995.

Underwriting performance worsened, in part due to high theft losses, and declining interest rates reduced investment income. Asemex reported an erosion of its business and nonrecurring items in 1996 that resulted in a net loss of 299 million pesos. During the first six months of 1997, the new Seguros Comercial America generated net income of 180 million pesos on 3.2 billion pesos of earned premiums.
Standard & Poor's believes the insurer maintains adequate financial strength despite absorbing the undercapitalized Asemex.

At year-end 1996, Asemex had a shortfall in its regulatory capital requirement of 740 million pesos, which was more than offset by Seguros Comercial America's 865 million pesos in excess of the minimum required capital. Standard & Poor's expects the solvency margin to improve as capital reserves are restored.

Majority ownership of the combined insurance company and its financial services subsidiaries is held by Pulsar Internacional, whose other investments include tobacco, agribusiness, printing and packaging, and concrete construction. U.S. investors include Travelers Group Inc. and Hicks, Muse, Tate & Furst Inc.

As competition increases from new entrants into the Mexican market, Standard & Poor's believes that the insurer's market position, cost structure, and relationships with large insurance brokers will be competitive advantages.

Over the near term, however, profitability from the Asemex business will be depressed by the need to create new reserves for incurred but not reported claims and to rebuild capital reserves Asemex released in 1995 to offset operating losses, Standard & Poor's said.
